newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand probes top Thai judge after U.S. drug suspect flees.
newsitem.headline: Thailand probes top Thai judge after U.S. drug suspect flees.

text.p: A senior Thai judge who granted bail to a man accused of masterminding the biggest heroin haul in U.S. history is being investigated after the suspect fled, Thai officials said on Wednesday.

Somchai Udomwong, the Deputy Chief Justice of the Criminal Court will be moved to an inactive post and the government will investigate why he signed a February 7 order freeing Li Yung Chung on five million baht ($192,308) bail, an official said.

"The Chief Justice is in the process of investigating the matter. (Somchai) will be transferred to an inactive post as soon as possible and we will set up a committee to look into the matter," Sooboon Vuthiwong, the judge originally responsible for Li's case, told Reuters.

Sooboon said Somchai had nothing to do with the case, and said Thai authorities were "very suspicious" about his reasons for granting Li bail because suspects awaiting extradition are not usually granted bail.
"If we find out he is guilty of accepting a bribe he will be kicked out of the judicial system and criminal charges will be placed against him," he said.
Somchai could not be reached for comment.

Li, also known by the Thai name Phongsak Rogjanasakul, is the main suspect in a drug haul worth up to $122 million and is wanted in the United States. Thai authorities believe he fled to Burma shortly after being granted bail.
The United States has said it was deeply concerned by the Thai court's decision to grant bail to Li, who has a Thai identity card but is of Chinese descent.
A U.S. government official welcomed the investigation of Somchai but said the United States was mainly interested in getting Li back and putting him on trial.
Thai foreign ministry officials said they were awaiting confirmation Li was in Burma before beginning talks with Rangoon to get him back to Thailand.

Opium warlord Khun Sa, also wanted on drugs charges in the United States, is living in Rangoon after surrendering to Burmese troops last year. Burma has vowed not to extradite him and said the government would deal with him in its own way.

Li was indicted by a New York court in May 1996 in connection with the largest heroin haul ever in the United States -- the seizure in 1991 of 486 kg (nearly 1,070 lb) of the drug in Hayward, California.
Drug officials put the U.S. street value between $180,000 to $250,000 per kg, making the haul worth $87.5 million to $122 million.

A U.S. government official said investigations by Thai and U.S. officials uncovered enough evidence to indict Li as the principal suspect behind the shipment, thought to be bound for New York from the infamous Golden Triangle region.

The Golden Triangle, where the borders of Thailand, Laos and Burma meet, was Khun Sa's home and the region where U.S. drugs officials say about 60 percent of the world's opium -- the raw material used to produce heroin -- is harvested.

After the indictment was issued, the United States requested Li's extradition from Thailand, the U.S. official said. Under a 1991 extradition treaty between the two countries, narcotics traffickers can be sent to the United States to face trial.
Thai officials arrested Li in July and were holding him for extradition.
